savedNotes.title: dbms Summary
savedNotes.content:
DBMS Module 1 – Easy Notes

1. Introduction to Database

What is Data?
Data means raw facts or values. Examples: numbers, names, marks, phone numbers. By itself, data may not give clear meaning.

  • Examples: 10, ABC, 95

What is a Record?

A record is a collection of related data.

  • Example: | Name | Phone | City |
  • Example: | Rahul | 9876543210 | Bangalore |

What is a Database?

A database is a collection of related data stored in an organized way.

  • Examples: Student database, Bank database, Hospital database, Railway reservation database
  • A database stores meaningful data.
  • Designed for a specific purpose.
  • Can be small or very large.

Terms Used in Tables

  • Row - Record / Tuple
  • Column - Field / Attribute
  • Table - Relation

2. DBMS (Database Management System)

What is DBMS?

DBMS is software used to:

  • Create databases
  • Store data
  • Update data
  • Retrieve data
  • Manage databases

Examples:

  • MySQL
  • Oracle
  • SQL Server
  • PostgreSQL

Functions of DBMS

  • Defining Database: Specifying data types, structure, constraints
  • Constructing Database: Storing data into storage devices
  • Manipulating Database: Operations like insert, update, delete, search, generate reports
  • Sharing Database: Allows many users to access the same database together

Database System

Database + DBMS software together are called a Database System.

3. File System vs Database System

File Processing System Problems:

  • Each department stored separate files
  • Same data repeated many times
  • Difficult to maintain

Problems:

  • Data duplication
  • Inconsistency
  • Difficult searching
  • Poor security

Database Approach

In DBMS:

  • Data is stored centrally
  • Multiple users can access the same data
  • Redundancy is reduced
  • Data becomes consistent

4. Characteristics of DBMS

  • Self-Describing Nature
  • Program-Data Independence
  • Data Abstraction
  • Multiple Views
  • Multiuser Access

Important Transaction Properties

  • Atomicity: Either all operations happen or none happen.
  • Isolation: Transactions work independently without affecting each other.

5. Users of DBMS

  • Database Administrator (DBA): Responsible for security, backup, permissions, performance
  • Database Designers: Design database structure
  • End Users: People who use the database

Types of End Users

  • Casual Users: Use database occasionally (e.g., managers)
  • Naive Users: Use predefined applications (e.g., bank tellers)
  • Sophisticated Users: Experts (e.g., engineers, analysts)
  • Standalone Users: Maintain personal databases.
  • System Analysts and Programmers: Analyze requirements and develop software applications

6. Advantages of DBMS

  • Controls Data Redundancy
  • Better Security
  • Backup and Recovery
  • Multiple User Interfaces
  • Integrity Constraints
  • Efficient Data Access
  • Represents Relationships

7. Disadvantages of DBMS

  • High cost
  • Requires hardware and software
  • Complex system
  • Needs trained people
  • Overhead for security and recovery

8. Data Models

What is a Data Model?

A data model defines the structure of data, relationships, and constraints.

Types of Data Models

  • High-Level / Conceptual Model
  • Physical Data Model
  • Representational / Relational Model

9. Schema and Instance

  • Schema: Structure/design of database (e.g., STUDENT(RollNo, Name, Age))
  • Instance: Actual data present at a particular time (e.g., | RollNo | Name |)

Schema Evolution

Changing database schema (e.g., adding a new column: Date_of_Birth).

10. Three Schema Architecture

Purpose: Separate users from physical storage.

  • Internal Level: Describes physical storage, files, indexes
  • Conceptual Level: Describes whole database structure, entities, relationships, constraints
  • External/View Level: Different users see different views

11. Data Independence

  • Logical Data Independence: Changes in conceptual schema should not affect user views.
  • Physical Data Independence: Changes in physical storage should not affect conceptual schema.

12. Database Languages

  • DDL (Data Definition Language): Used to define database structure (e.g., CREATE, ALTER, DROP)
  • DML (Data Manipulation Language): Used to manipulate data (e.g., INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT)
  • SDL (Storage Definition Language): Defines internal storage.
  • VDL (View Definition Language): Defines user views.
  • SQL: Most DBMS use SQL (Structured Query Language).

13. Types of DML

  • High-Level DML: Easy to use, works on multiple records together (e.g., SQL queries).
  • Low-Level DML: Works record by record, usually embedded in programming languages.

14. DBMS Interfaces

  • Menu-Based Interface: Uses menus.
  • Forms-Based Interface: Users fill forms.
  • GUI (Graphical User Interface): Uses graphics and diagrams.
  • Natural Language Interface: Users type commands in normal language.
  • Speech Interface: Uses voice input/output.

15. DBMS Components

  • Query Processor: Processes SQL queries.
  • Query Optimizer: Chooses the best execution method.
  • Storage Manager: Controls stored data.
  • Buffer Manager: Manages memory buffers.
  • Backup & Recovery Manager: Handles recovery after failure.

16. Database Utilities

  • Loading: Loads existing data into the database.
  • Backup: Creates backup copies.
  • Reorganization: Improves storage performance.
  • Performance Monitoring: Checks database performance.

17. ER Model (Entity Relationship Model)

ER Model is used for database design.

  • Entity
  • Attribute
  • Relationship

18. Entity

An entity is a real-world object (e.g., Student, Employee, Car, Course).

19. Attributes

Attributes describe entities (e.g., EMPLOYEE: Name, Age, Salary).

20. Types of Attributes

  • Simple Attribute
  • Composite Attribute
  • Single-Valued Attribute
  • Multi-Valued Attribute
  • Stored Attribute
  • Derived Attribute
  • NULL Value

21. Entity Type and Entity Set

  • Entity Type: Definition of entities (e.g., EMPLOYEE)
  • Entity Set: Collection of all entities (e.g., All employees in a company)

22. Key Attribute

Attribute used to uniquely identify entities (e.g., Employee_ID).

23. Weak Entity

Weak entity does not have its own key; it depends on another entity (e.g., DEPENDENT depends on EMPLOYEE).

24. Relationship

Relationship connects entities (e.g., EMPLOYEE works for DEPARTMENT).

25. Degree of Relationship

  • Binary Relationship: Between 2 entities (e.g., EMPLOYEE — DEPARTMENT)
  • Ternary Relationship: Between 3 entities (e.g., SUPPLIER — PART — PROJECT)

26. Recursive Relationship

Entity related to itself (e.g., EMPLOYEE supervises EMPLOYEE).

27. Cardinality Constraints

Shows maximum relationship participation.

  • 1:1
  • 1:N
  • M:N

28. Participation Constraints

  • Total Participation: Every entity must participate.
  • Partial Participation: Participation is optional.

29. Attributes of Relationships

Relationships can also have attributes (e.g., HOURS in WORKS_ON relationship).

30. Naming Rules in ER Model

  • Use meaningful names
  • Use singular names
  • Entity names in uppercase
  • Attribute names start with capital letters

31. UML Class Diagram

In UML: Entity → Class, Entity instance → Object, Class contains: class name, attributes, operations.

32. Important Quick Differences

  • Schema vs Instance: Structure vs Actual data
  • DDL vs DML: Defines structure vs Manipulates data

Final Quick Revision

  • Database: Collection of related data
  • DBMS: Software to manage databases
  • Metadata: Data about data
  • Schema: Database structure
  • Instance: Current data in database
  • Entity: Real-world object
  • Attribute: Property of entity
  • Relationship: Connection between entities
  • Key Attribute: Uniquely identifies an entity
  • SQL: Language used in DBMS

Very Important Exam Topics

  • DBMS advantages and disadvantages
  • File system vs DBMS
  • Data models
  • Three-schema architecture
  • Data independence
  • DDL and DML
  • ER model
  • Types of attributes
  • Cardinality constraints
  • Weak entity
  • Keys

Small Memory Tricks

  • DBMS Functions: D-C-M-S (Define, Construct, Manipulate, Share)
  • Three Schema Levels: E-C-I (External, Conceptual, Internal)
